utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you informed by Mr. Lukic or any senior member of the police administration of the arming of ethnic Serb in reserve police squads during the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that but those were not detachments the reserve police, but reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These were ethnic Serb civilians in villages and settlements who were given weapons ostensibly to depend the village and settlements?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were members of the reserve police force and of the reserve force in the army who were issued weapons, and they, as part of the reserve police squads, were supposed to protect their villages against terrorist incursions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's a difference which has been explained to us in court before between a reserve policeman, a reservist, and a member of these reserve police squads. The members of the reserve police squads were not reserve policemen, were they?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not policemen, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you ever aware that these members of the reserve police squads were sometimes used in joint MUP/VJ operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. I'm sure that they were not used for any joint army and police actions. The reserve police squads' purview was to mount a defence. They could only protect the parts of the villages inhabited by non-Albanians, or if those villages were purely Serbian in ethnical terms, they defended and protected those villages, and nothing else. They never launched any attacks. They never went to other villages to attack them. They didn't provide any support to the army or to the police in any anti-terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You did see -- I did show you yesterday, a document, an order by General Pavkovic engaging MUP and VJ forces in which he also engaged civilians to help in a blockade. You are saying you weren't aware of that aspect of the operation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the armed Serbs, or rather, we are talking about the reserve police squads. Let us focus on that now. Reserve police squads were never used to act in concert with the army and the police in the execution of any tasks, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were armed ethnic Serb civilians who were not members of either the VJ or the police, the MUP, used in any of these operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you discuss the arming of ethnic Serbs with other members of what has been described as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is a category where people were armed as part of the Territorial Defence or the civilian protection, but this was done by the military structures. I was not aware of it. I was not told about it. I was more focused on the protection of the villages against terrorist attacks, and reserve police squads were tasked with that. So the policy of en block, en masse arming of the Serb civilians is unfamiliar to me. Whether it was done in accordance with some military rules or a decision of the defence minister, I really don't know the details, and I can't really say anything because I'm not qualified. I know that those civilians were not involved in any offensive operations targeting the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, let's save some time. I'll ask the question again, and I'll just ask you to answer it. Did you discuss or participate in discussions regarding the arming of ethnic Serb civilians with other members of the so-called Joint Command? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't discuss it with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that the army was involved in arming Serb -- you said, maybe there was something done under some military rules. And there's a category of people who were armed, but this was done by the military structure. Were the reserve police squads commanded by members of the MUP that were ultimately down the chain of command subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let's clear the last question up. Nobody was subordinate to me. That's the first thing. It's the key issue, in fact, to my mind. Secondly, it is quite likely that some of the active police officers were in charge of some reserve police squads, that would be a police officer who was from that village or from a neighbouring village, and it was his task to provide some kind of a professional support or assistance to the population and to the reserve police squad to help defend them against the terrorists. I can tell you that for a number of years before this period there was a lot of pressure on the Serb people, the non-Albanian people in general there. Two, three, or five years before the events that we are talking about, we would send four or five police officers to guard a single house surrounded by Albanian houses in a village, and those police officers lived in the same household with the villagers to protect them against the attacks and the pressure exerted by the extremist Albanians in order to ensure their bare survival. So the police provided support in various ways to protect the people that were under pressure of this or that kind. And at that time when the entire territory of Kosovo, for all intents and purposes, was heavily under the influence of terrorists, it was decided that this would be a good way to protect the villages. But you have to understand this, this is very clear, to protect the villages, none of these people who had weapons went to other villages to kill Albanians or whatever. It was their task to remain in their village and defend it, and they never were engaged in any offensive operations whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I glean from your answer, Mr. Djordjevic, that you are saying that quite likely a police officer from the village or from a neighbouring village might have provided some kind of professional support. Do you not know that these reserve police squads were placed under the command of the local police station, the chief of a local police station?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's confusion here. They were never placed under command of any of the local officers, police officers, police stations, or SUP chiefs. They were in touch with the police station. The police station provided them with radio stations, weapons, so that if there was an attack, they could call the police station and the police station could then take measures to protect them against the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look quickly at document 1052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is coming up, could I mention that the transcript at page 2, line 1, shows two questions in a row with no answer recorded. There was an answer. It may be incorporated into one of the questions, or it may have been missed altogether. If that could be checked and confirmed when the transcript is being verified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The members of the reserve police squads, these villagers, they were not policemen, neither regular policemen nor reserve policemen, that is what you had said before?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or rather, some of them were members of the reserve force, but at that time those people were not engaged as the members of the reserve force of the police station, so they were on the list of the reserve force, but at that point in time, they were doing jobs that had nothing to do with the police station work, simply to protect the village. They did not -- they were not entitled to anything, to DSA, to salaries as MUP members while they were doing that. Some of them may have been on the list of the reserve force, but they were not used in that capacity. There was a major difference between the two categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we have the wrong document before the Court. I wanted P1052. And could we move on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from Major-General Lukic of the 10th of January [sic], 1998, to the commanders of the departments of the interior for Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, he says: "To organise the defence of village with the newly-formed reserve police squads." And next he says: "Carry out combat training of all RPOs. And for every RPO, create a file which include, among other things, the training plan, communications plan, ammunition renewal plan, staff control plan at a municipal level." Does this document indicate to you -- and also if I could remind you of the testimony of the former SUP chief Cvetic that these RPOs were organised, managed, and controlled by the MUP, by the local police departments?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here quite clearly what obligations are imposed on the police stations where police squads were to be set up, so the MUP staff here informs the secretariats and the police stations that they should do some things to ensure that the members of the reserve force, or rather, the reserve police squad, could defend their villages. And in this regard, a plan, combat training plan was drafted. This combat training plan involved infantry weapons training in order to make sure that the members of those squads could actually use those weapons. It also included various measures to fortify the village, to defend it against the terrorists. Also the communications plan in order to ensure that if the terrorists attack the villages, they could call the police stations in order for the police stations to be able to assist them in case of a terrorist attack. So all those obligations imposed on the police stations by this order, in fact, concern logistics, training, and equipping members of the reserve police squads in order to make sure that they would be able to defend their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is, does this document not remind you or indicate to you that these local police stations were responsible for organising, training, and managing these reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript: The date should be the 10th of July, 1998, and the transcript reads the 10th of January. Page 6, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. There was a question asked, you are waiting on an answer, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Could I get the question again because now I lost the thread.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does the document remind you or indicate to you that the local OUPs, the local departments of interior were responsible for the management and organisation of these reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have two questions here. The first concerns management, and the other, organisation. The police stations were duty-bound to provide assistance to the reserve police squads to train them so that they would be able to respond independently to terrorist attacks. But the police stations did not exert control over those reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at 1053. P1053.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a document from one commander, Radica Nastic, of the military department of Kosovska Mitrovica, and he speaks of training of the reserve formation of the Ministry of Interior in the villages of -- in the municipality of Vucitrn. Did the VJ co-ordinate with the MUP in the arming and training of these members of the reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, members of the reserve police squads included some of the members of the reserve force of the Yugoslav army, locals, people who lived in those villages. So the reserve police squads did not comprise only members of the reserve police force. Some of the people there in those squads were also part of the Yugoslav army reserve force. I think there were cases where the Yugoslav army provided assistance to the MUP to train the reserve force. It was always the case because these people were really highly qualified to deal with some topics as part of the training, so I think this was what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many infantry weapons, or approximately how many infantry weapons were distributed to members of these reserve police squads in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really give you the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably to all the squad members, or rather, all the squad members or most of them were issued weapons. It was possible that each squad, let's say, was given ten rifles and then they could use it in shifts. So I don't know how many pieces; I don't know the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't the co-ordination of the arming and training of these groups by both the VJ and the MUP organised through the Joint Command or organised as a result of decisions made by the so-called Joint Command whose meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such a decision being taken, but there is the instruction of the leaders of the MUP staff how the defence of villages should be organised through reserve police squads and the military in accordance with relevant rules and regulations as well as categories applied there probably dealt with their own reservists in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P1054. Is that before -- is that the one before the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a report from SUP chief Cvetic on the reserve police squads in this area that he sent to the MUP staff in Pristina -- to the head of the MUP staff in Pristina. And he said that in the SUP area, this is the first part of the document, 41 reserve police branch station RPOs have been organised with a total of 1.374 members. He says a total of 1.000 long-barreled weapons have been delivered of which 735 have been distributed. And he goes on to give a breakdown of the leadership and the organisation of these reserve police squads which he describes as reserve police branch stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you move on to page 2 both in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to look quickly at the document. And it's pretty much the same going through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could move to the last page in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that you can hear me even without a microphone. Could we first see the second page because it couldn't be seen on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to the end of the document, please. Could we move to the end of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Signed by Colonel Cvetic as the head of the secretariat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't want to bother you, I'm sorry, but the second page of the document doesn't match the second page of the English version. If we go back to the second page of the B/C/S version, you can see the Roman numerals II and III, and in the English version you won't find them. Under II and III, that is, under Zvecan, there is this part with a heading "Zvecan" is missing altogether in the Serbian version so that there are items Roman II and Roman III. Both versions match here, but under II and III, there is nothing in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What you are missing is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. And could we go to the end of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Signed by Mr. Cvetic here in which he indicates the total number of the weapons that were delivered to these persons. Does this not indicate to you, Mr. Djordjevic, that the local police were responsible for the management of these local police squads?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the notion of management has about a dozen components. I'm not sure what you mean. I said that the police secretariat -- some police stations provided help, and they equipped reserve police squads. And here we see that there were also members of the military reserve forces, and these police squads were equipped. There was training and preparation for those people to be able to use the weapons they were given to defend themselves against terrorists. But that doesn't mean that the police station manages these squads. But could I ask for the first page to be put back on the screen so that we can see the date when this was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 1st of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time and before, I was in Belgrade, and these were duties performed by the staff. They were responsible for that. And even later during my stay down there and after getting acquainted with these documents, I can say that I have never seen any of these documents. They weren't forwarded to me, and I don't know anything about this. This reads that -- or this shows how these squads were established, and it shows some principles. But this all took place outside the scope of my stay at Kosovo, and the staff acted in accordance with instructions and their obligations. And they were involved in co-ordination with the military and equipping the police squad, et cetera, but this is all outside of my stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at P975.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is dated the 30th of July, within your stay. This is Major-General Lukic's dispatch to the SUP chief for Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. 30th of July, 1998. He says: "Please find enclosed extracts from the register of weapons issued by the Army of Yugoslavia to citizens engaged in reserve police stations to defend villages and cities in the municipalities under your secretariat's jurisdiction." And if we look at the next page, you see him give a breakdown of the municipalities for a total of 7.436 in the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. This one is in the time-frame when you were there, Mr. Djordjevic. You still maintain that you don't know about this?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I knew nothing about it. I said that I know in principle but I don't know this information. This is the first time I've seen this breakdown. You can believe me. I didn't get the instructions issued by the Chief of Staff to the secretariats in the field, nor did I know anything about that. I only knew that reserve police squads were established, I knew their composition, I knew that they were armed and that they were preparing to defend themselves against the terrorists. But this summary and the instructions given by the Chief of Staff to the secretariats in accordance with the obligations of the Chief of Staff, well, this is the first time I've seen these instructions and this report. We can see what these instructions are like, and it is clearly outlined who is charged with distributing weapons. But I didn't decide about this nor did I control the work of the staff in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You knew about the arming of these reserve police squads, Mr. Djordjevic, from your participation in meetings of the so-called Joint Command; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. I knew that they were being armed through my contacts with the staff. And I didn't learn that at staff meetings. There may have been mention of that too, but it was no decision of that staff or that Joint Command, as you call it, to establish reserve police squads. The reserve police squads, as far as I know, were established based on the decision of the MUP staff, and then all these steps took place through synchronising all activities and their training, equipping, and preparing for defence. The basic issue is that these police squads were not used for offensive actions, but only to defend their bare lives. I don't know if you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you keep going way beyond the questions I ask you and using time unnecessarily in saying things two or three times. The next question is this - and maybe I should show you a document when I ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P886.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the document in front of you. That's the minutes of the MUP staff of the Joint Command meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We could go to 20th of July, and in English I think that's page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you look at that, just scroll back to the pages earlier to satisfy yourself that you attended that meeting, according to these records. Isn't that correct, you were there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 20th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first date here is the 22nd of July, that must have been the 22nd of August maybe. On the 20th of July, 1998, no meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Two eight. 28.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something else. The interpretation that I received was the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could go to the last page of that day, which is page 18 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic is recorded to have said: "Check the training - 52.250 barrels have been issued." Do you know what he was referring to? What were you discussing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant there. 52.000 barrels, I really don't know what he meant. Let me see what this is. I can't find Andjelkovic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the last entry for that day.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but the pages are oriented differently. The 28th --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we expand the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move quickly, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, here, Andjelkovic, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were you discussing that that made reference to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read, here, what the minute-taker put down. There's a breakdown by communities, authorities, distribution, inspection. I don't know how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. He said "check the training - 52.250 barrels have been issued." What does that mean? What were you discussing when he said that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how am I supposed to say what we spoke about? The one who took these minutes put down what was interesting to him. And I'm now supposed to interpret -- an inspection is mentioned, then some guy Andjelkovic is supposed to give orders. I don't really understand this. I don't -- what is noted here isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And if that's your answer, you can just say so, you don't know, without us --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to know, but this is less than precise. 52.250, if I'm not mistaken, rifles were distributed and some kind of inspection is taking place. I really don't know for which needs these rifles were distributed. It doesn't -- it can't be inferred based on this, so I really can't say anything useful, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you see that, I think, from your answer we can take it that he was referring to rifles. That day you were out in the field, that is a day you were in Malisevo and you missed a MUP staff meeting with the permission of the minister, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend the meeting at which the minister was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at the minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's P688.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here I can see that General Rade attended, it's probably Rade Markovic. So he also attends this meeting of… what you call the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Really I'm not asking you that. Let's look at P688. Minutes of the MUP staff meeting of the 20th of July, attended by the minister himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to get an idea of the attendees.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 7 in English, and I believe that's the penultimate page in B/C/S. But let's go to page 7 in the English, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have before you the record of the intervention of major -- or Captain Pesic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you read it? This is what Captain Pesic reported to the minister and the other senior members of the MUP present. He said: "Weapons have been distributed to 54.683 persons. The MUP issued 12.170 weapons; the VJ, 34.716; the MUP of the Republic of Serbia brought another 5.070 pieces of weapons to the territory of Kosovo, and they are being issued. When all of this is finished, about 60.000 persons have been issued weapons." Now, as the chief of the RJB, were you aware that it was that quantity of weapons, infantry weapons, over 50.000, that was distributed to the RPOs in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with this figure, but from this report I gather that this is the figure they speak about. But while I was down there, I didn't know that this number of persons was involved and nor did I know the relative shares given by the MUP and the VJ respectively. The -- I did not know these concrete figures at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But this involved a significant amount of logistic operations, logistics from the headquarters of the ministry, since we see here that weapons are being moved from out of Kosovo into Kosovo to arm these people. Wouldn't you or shouldn't you be aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the weapons are distributed to the organisational units of the MUP. So, in a way, it was a regular way of equipping the secretariat in accordance with the needs reported. Each of these weapons is registered so that relevant information is available. I believe that this is a regular obligation which was necessary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You saw that many of these weapons from a previous document I showed you included machine-guns. The evidence of Mr. Cvetic is that these citizens would keep these guns in their homes. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some of those people really did take those weapons home, or wherever it was that their security service was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the next page of this document, and I think if you could hold it there, the next page in English. And I think it remains the same page in B/C/S. I think it's the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Lukic also says, reports to the minister: "We are also arming citizens in towns, and plans for defending towns have been drawn up." You see that? Now, the question is --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having regard to what is reported here to the minister contained in this document, weren't you aware that these reserve police squads were being managed by the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said ten times the term "management" or whatever the term is being used in the interpretation, but MUP and the police station did not manage the reserve police squads. I've already said that logistics issues, equipping, training, organisation of the defence and so on, but if you want to say that they were part of the ministry and that the ministry ordered them to do this or that, well, that was not done. They had a very specific task, to defend their villages. The MUP provided them with assistance, by equipping them, providing them with communications equipment and some training, but MUP did not manage it, did not control those squads. And secondly, Minister Stojiljkovic himself says here, since I can see that you are reading the data from a report, Please send this report to the Serbian MUP. So he asks Captain Pesic to send this report to him, and he is asking him about 250 radio stations, or rather, he is asking Lukic about that. So I'm just saying you can see what kind of orders the minister is issuing and what kind of information he is asking those who were present at the meeting to give him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look quickly at another document. D340.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a VJ document dated the 2nd of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in the English, and I don't have the B/C/S page, but that is item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see here at the last bullet point under "experiences gained" we see: "The distribution of weapons to citizens loyal to the FRY has made it possible for large-scale resistance against the terrorists to be organised." I just point out that part of it to you, Mr. Djordjevic, to ask you if you remember that this being a coordinated activity between the MUP and the VJ, it was -- it received it's direction from the Joint Command? Do you accept that or disagree?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at the Joint Command minutes briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's P886. Meeting of the 29th of July, 1998. 29th of July, 1998. English page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think it's page 22 also in your copy. Last entry, and before we discuss that, can you just look at the document and tell us if you were present at that meeting, if you are recorded as being present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And General Lukic is quoted here as saying that: "Weapons were distributed today in Vitina (1.100) Kosovska Kamenica, training has not been conducted." You see the last entry on that page?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th of July, General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the English version -- well, I can't see what is written there, but if I'm not mistaken, he is talking about 3.000 uniforms for the reserve force, I'm now talking about the English version. He is not talking about weapons or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll read it to you, the last entry for that day on the report, so possibly not General Lukic: "Weapons were distributed today in Vitina (1.100) Kosovska Kamenica, training has not been conducted yet." Were you at that meeting discussing --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- discussing the distribution of weapons to ethnic Serb civilians and their training? Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, this is what is stated in this report. If everything that is recorded here is correct, yes, I was present there on that day. But now what categories are we talking about here? Whoever took the minutes, wrote down whatever he thought was important. He says, Today they gave weapons in Vitina 1.100 and in Kosovska Kamenica, and there is a no other information, whether it was distributed to the army, to the reserve police, to whoever; it really is not stated. And what was the basis for those weapons being issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. You were there at this discussion. Those are those notes. Do you remember, and could you fill us in on what you were talking about in respect to these weapons? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how am I supposed to remember after ten years? I agree and I accept that this was discussed, but there's no decision here to that effect. Weapons had been distributed earlier on whatever basis, and this is just a report informing those present that the weapons had been distributed. And now as for on the basis of what decision, it's not stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at another entry. Page 55, the meeting for the 20th of August, 1998. And page 55 in English, page 56, I think, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And firstly, could you confirm for us whether or not you were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that I was present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we see Mr. Minic speaking. And the third -- one, two three, four, the fourth bullet point in this speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps you could expanded the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Says --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourth bullet point: "Engage the Serbs in those villages." If that's the one you mean? "Recruit the Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Recruit the Serbs in those villages (list the villages) and organise a meeting with the village commanders." Again, noted as if this is a command. Do you recall that discussion at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is the record of the meeting, it might very well be, but I can't remember. How am I supposed to remember? But this term, the village commander, it was not used; I'm sure about that. As to why it was used here, I can't tell you. It's beyond me. There was discussion about the situation in the villages, the problems that they encountered, the attacks on the villages, the defence that was mounted. Those issues were discussed. Information was exchanged. This was not controversial at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but can I ask you this: In a situation when there is very high electric ethnic tensions, if you are the chief of police, as the most senior policeman, if you are aware that one ethnicity or members of one ethnicity are being armed with machine-guns, 50.000 plus machine-guns, and other infantry weapons, weren't you interested, at least, to closely monitor that situation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, on the eve of this period that we're talking about, and even during that period, 50 per cent of Serbia was controlled, occupied by the terrorists. The non-Albanian population was concerned. They were afraid for their lives. They were moving out of this area under the pressure from the terrorists. And now we are talking about whether those Serbs were supposed to defend themselves or not. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know, maybe you didn't understand the question. I'm not saying persons shouldn't be defended. I'm really asking you to address what I consider to be a very worrisome thing about your memory, you don't recall what other people might consider to be important things. Here we have a situation when there is very strong ethnic tension between the Serbian population and the Albanian population. Your police force is involving -- involved in arming one group to the tune of up to 60.000 weapons, light-infantry weapons, but including machine-guns, which these people keep at their homes. Were you not interested in monitoring this situation very carefully?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. The situation was monitored very closely. As was the situation that resulted in 100.000 pieces of heavy weaponry, machine-guns, and other heavy weaponry crossing into Kosovo from the Albanian territory, that was later used by the terrorists to attack civilians. So that was the situation. The Serbs did not take up arms to defend themselves because they wanted to do that, because they were happy to do that, because that was the only way for them to save their lives. This is why it was done. This is why those people were trained so that while we were waiting for the regular forces to come in so that they would be able to defend themselves. But let me tell you this: 60 citizens had been abducted from Orahovac. Those people were worried about their family members. They didn't know what was going on. They wanted somebody to go down there and to hold a meeting. I went down there; I had a meeting with the municipality chief and the police chief and Mr. Matkovic was there. People were demanding arms. They said, We want to have arms to defend ourselves. I didn't want to allow that. I said the police and the army would look for your family members, and you cannot be given weapons and do those things on your own. And now we have a situation that -- where they had to save their lives. And it is very difficult to find a clever solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So did you receive any report on the work or on the engagement of these armed ethnic Serbs and the use of these weapons with which they had been supplied by members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the weapons were used only for self-defence, and for no other reason while I was down there. The weapons were not used for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive -- I'm just repeating the question. Did you receive any report in your capacity as chief of police on the use of those weapons that had been distributed to these people?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ask for any?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In light of my position, did I not receive any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But in light of your position as chief of the police, did you ask for any?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've seen that the minister asked for very specific reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the minutes of that meeting. I didn't ask for any reports, because I did not have any knowledge to the effect that there was any abuse of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P1051.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a July 1998 document, a Joint Command Kosovo and Metohija document. Entitled "Instructions for the defence of inhabited places (temporary)." We move to the first page, or the next page. It says: "The goal of the instructions is to ensure in accordance with the purpose and capabilities of the police forces defending towns, their acquiring of adequate knowledge and application of standardised positions and procedures in preparing and organising combat operations and unarmed combat and resistance." Were you aware of the circulation of this document in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. I don't know whether it's from 1998 at all. I didn't see the date. I was not aware of these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: July 1998. Same time as the meetings that I just showed you were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we move to the next page, page 3 in the English. And I think it might be the next page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the date is crucial here. Yes, it is July, but there are 31 days in July. That's why I'm not familiar with it. It may have been issued on the 10th or the 15th of July. We don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Under 2, you see that? "In specific conditions, the forces for the defence of cities and inhabited areas are the MUP units which unify all the forces in inhabited areas and organise, lead, and perform combat operations. They change their composition depending on the size and significance of the town." So --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "will exercise b/d;" that's what it is in this item. I think that the army drafted the instructions because they use this kind of terminology, b/d combat operations. But it's possible that this was all done in the beginning of July or in mid-July when I was not there at all. And that's why I am not able to remember this document. The document itself, I know that there was discussion about defence of the towns and villages and that terrorist actions were not carried out in the towns. There were some indications that there would be some terrorists attacks here or there, but I'm really not aware of this document. But the way in which this document is drafted indicates that it was drafted by somebody in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a Joint Command document, and you testified about how these documents were drafted before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7 in the English document under item 5. If you could find item 5 in the B/C/S and page 7 in the English document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 5, "Command." It's a military term, pure and simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Command and contrast." Could you read this first paragraph aloud, please?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command and control is an activity of a staff organising the defence of a town. The commander of the unit organising the defence is a police officer, and he shall exercise command over the engaged forces. The commander shall be responsible for the execution of the tasks that were set." When I read this, I'm completely unfamiliar with this document. And, in fact, I'm not familiar with the system of the defence of a town. You set up the defence of a town and you put a police officer in charge of the defence, well, that's really something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall, I showed you another document in which General Lukic himself had ordered setting up of units to be armed for defence of towns. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at another Joint Command meeting. P690.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is one that was shown to you during your examination-in-chief. The record of a meeting of the MUP staff for the 3rd of November, 1998, chaired by General Lukic. Did you attend this meeting, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There, in item 1, they discuss some agreements you had signed, and if we move straightaway to item 8. This is page 3 of the English document. Could you just read that. You can read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He says, and this is -- I remind you, this is a discussion of how to behave now that there were observers, KVM observers, as a result of the agreements discussed in paragraph 1 of this document. He says: "Make sure that Serbs and members of the RPOs do not misuse weapons, let off guns at weddings, celebrations at Slava, farewell parties, and so on. Do not carry weapons or show them in public in the presence of the members of the mission." So were you -- before I ask that question, can I just ask you, does that statement, the record of the statement in this official MUP document, indicate to you that these armed ethnic Serbs were under the control of the police in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it doesn't show that they were not under their control. Here he warns that those who have weapons, if they misuse them, will be subject to legal action. So they must not shoot at weddings, Slavas, et cetera. And it's along these lines that he insists on a legal behaviour. Here it says: "Insist that Serbs and members of the RPO do not" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do not misuse weapons. But, Mr. Djordjevic, he does not say that they would be subject to legal action. Certainly not in this paragraph. He is telling them, telling these senior police officers to restrain these people because the mission, the KVM mission, has arrived. Isn't that what he is doing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. This isn't what this is about at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Djurdjic, there's an answer being given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with your conclusion. Here, the Chief of Staff warns -- the head of staff is warning the chiefs of the SUPs of misuse. He insists that the weapons should not be misused and should not be carried publicly. I don't know how else to interpret what I can read here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed this for several times, but I didn't want to react. Parts of the text are not interpreted literally. And irrespective of the time constraints, I would ask my learned friend Mr. Stamp to quote literally. This literally says "insist that Serbs and members of the RPO do not misuse weapons, let off guns at wettings, celebrations of Slava, farewell parties, and so on." If we do quote, let us quote accurately and then subsequently elicit an answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I think I read that at page 27, lines 21 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I'm now going beyond a reading, literally, of this document, Mr. Djordjevic. I want you to understand that, that I am suggesting to you that what General Lukic is telling these police commanders is that they should make sure that these armed Serb civilians refrain from using the weapons in the manner discussed, letting them off at weddings, celebrations of Slava, farewell parties, and so on, because of the presence of the mission?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This clearly says, and this is part of the regular jobs of the police: police and -- as part of their regular duties, establishes offences committed by misuse of weapons. Here he says that the weapons should not be misused, and he says, apart from that, they should not carry weapons publicly. And they shouldn't show their weapons in the presence of the members of the mission. That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he goes on to say: "Tell them not to state the fact that the Serbs are armed, and to explain this fact if they must, using the excuse that it is only members of the guard who are armed." This is just General Lukic's instructions to the police chiefs. Wasn't he telling the police chiefs that the massive arming of Serb civilians in Kosovo should be concealed from the international observers?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is pointing out here that at the guard points, one piece of weaponry is used; and he also insists, as far as I can tell, in the discharge of their duties, rather than individuals bringing weapons that were distributed to them. And the fact that Serbs are armed -- this doesn't say that they should conceal this fact from the members of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, you are reading the document. I'll ask you the question another way. Wouldn't you agree with me that this last sentence could be interpreted to mean that the commanders of the police should ensure that this massive arming of the Serb civilians is concealed by the -- concealed from the international KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I read it, the basic task is prevent a misuse of these weapons and see to it that the weapons are used exclusively for guarding in the framework of the RPO. And one piece of weaponry should be used. And weapons shouldn't be publicly displayed in the presence of the mission members. So he is pointing out that a professional conduct is required with regard to these weapons and that weapons should only be used for exercising guard duty at these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when he says: "Tell them not to state the fact that the Serbs are armed and to explain this fact, if they must, using the excuse that it is only members of the guards that are armed." I suggest to you, Mr. Djordjevic, it is an effort to conceal from the international observers the fact that the police in Kosovo were engaged in a very, very dangerous -- what was known to be a very, very dangerous programme of arming one ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am wondering if that's a convenient time, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the break now, Mr. Stamp, and resume at 25 minutes past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we have a look at P902 again. And that is the minutes of the collegium meeting of the 21st of January, 1999. And go straight to page 16 in the English and 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, can I ask you, Mr. Djordjevic, wasn't it an obvious fact of which the leadership of the armed force of Serbia was aware that arming civilians could have very dangerous results?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Do you see -- I can tell you without us having to scroll through this that this is the contribution of the chief of security, the VJ General Dimitrijevic, and do you see where he says in the sixth paragraph of page 15 before you, sixth paragraph from the top, he says: "Bearing in mind the number of people owning or having been distributed weapons, there is a realistic possibility on the Serbian and Montenegrin side of the Serbian population organising itself to offer resistance and of an increasing emergence of radical forces." You see where the general has said that? Sixth paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is January, now, 1999, weren't you aware, just as he is, that the arming, with that type of weapon and that many weapons, of an ethnic group in circumstances where there is strong ethnic tension had many dangers or had, at least, a danger of the group becoming subject to the influence of what he calls "radical forces," and of members of that group committing crimes on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay at Kosovo in 1998, no one member of these armed groups of citizens committed any crime with the weapons towards a citizen of other ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How do you know --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic's view and assessment -- I was down there in 1998. I said during my stay down there, no one member of the Serbian people, thus armed, as we discussed, killed any one ethnic Albanian. And on the other side, we had hundreds of people who were killed or kidnapped by the terrorists. And the general is sitting in his cabinet, and he is thinking about what could happen. Well, if they had had nuclear weapons, they could have used them against each other, and in accordance with this line of thinking. It's very easy sitting in your office and thinking, while down there they’d brought in recoilless guns, machine-guns, and mortars, and all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am merely asking, weren't you aware of the dangers of what you were doing which required that you should closely monitor this situation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I didn’t do that. And whether or not I was aware of the danger, that is a very general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But were you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. Was I aware of that. If there are weapons -- I mean, there are nuclear weapons, so there might be a nuclear war. I had no concrete information showing that the Serb people would self-organise in spite of the existence of strong police and military units to defend itself against the Albanians. When people came to me to ask for weapons so that they could go off themselves and look for their kidnapped family and friends, I never consented to do that. And you now want me to comment the way of thinking of General Dimitrijevic who was sitting in Belgrade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move to February, and you were down in Kosovo, in Pristina, at that time. Let's look at the minutes of 17th of February. P85. You were shown those minutes by counsel during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at the time. I was there on that day, so I attended a meeting on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And one of the first things you mentioned when you were shown this document in chief was that you did not know of a staff plans to carry out three mopping-up operations until that meeting, or am I misinterpreting what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of these actions. I didn't know who was planning what.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This action involves some, what, 5.000 policemen in Kosovo, that was a significant proportion of the policemen in Kosovo. And your evidence is that you had no awareness of a plan involving 5.000 policemen in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there is a clear order showing who was duty-bound to plan, to order, or to execute certain tasks in Kosovo when it comes to combat or anti-terrorist activities, but I was not the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You didn't know --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who was charged to do that -- of course I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said, and this is in the -- at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe we could scroll down a little bit in both copies so we can see the entirety of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "The staff plans, when it is ordered, to carry out three mopping-up operations in Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas, and has allotted 4.000 policemen, around 70 policemen of the OPG, and around 900 police reservists." And you also said you had no idea as to what he was referring to when he said "when it is ordered"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clearly says the staff planned to execute it "when it is ordered." I couldn't order the staff anything, nor did I ever issue an order to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Listen to the question. Listen to the question, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am listening to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know who would order the staff to proceed, to implement, this plan involving some 5.000 policemen?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff acted in accordance with the orders issued by the minister, and I was not part of that process. The minister ordered the staff to co-operate with the VJ in the execution of plans of which we have spoken aloud here, worked out by the Pristina Corps to combat the terrorists. I had no authority over the staff of any kind. I knew, at a general level, what the duties of the staff were, from that decision, and that's all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I want us to move quickly. Is your answer that it was the minister who would order the staff? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff was duty-bound, in accordance with the decision of the minister, to plan activities, command all forces that it had at its disposal, and it reported to the minister about it. It was responsible to the minister. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the RPOs, if you look a little bit further up in this paragraph, we see him referring to the RPOs. You see: "Reserve police stations in nearly all villages inhabited by Serbs are very active. The service has increased its activities in towns." And later on, and this is near the end of the page in English, and I think we should move on to page 2 in B/C/S, he also says: "Meetings have been held with all the RPOs, and they were attended by General Momcilo Stojanovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Blagoje Pesic. Their work and engagement have been assessed as good, aimed at protecting the people." Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just about the translation or interpretation actually, the transcript constantly reads reserve police "stations," whereas actually this is about reserve police "squads." And I believe that Mr. Stamp has also read that. But the reserve police "station" has somehow made their way to the transcript several times where they really should be reserve police "squad."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's correct. It should be reserve police squad, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, police squad. On the previous page, you said two things that -- or, rather, two things are stressed. First, activities in the framework of the RPOs, that is, reserve police squads; and then there are the activities of the secretariat. So I would ask to you return to the previous page in order to avoid misunderstandings, because you merged these two things so it can be understood as --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we return to the first page, I read a passage near the middle of that paragraph where he said: "RPOs in nearly all the villages inhabited by Serbs are active. The service has increased its activities in towns." And at the bottom of the page in English --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a period here, please. These are two distinct things. So there's one sentence reads RPO in nearly all villages inhabited by Serbs are very active. And the other sentence reads: The service has increased its activities in towns. And on the other page, what you say about Momcilo Stojanovic and Pesic as members of a team, this refers to the first part, the intensive activities of the RPOs. So maybe we should keep that apart and then maybe comment the reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We are talking about the RPOs now. Now, who is -- or, who was -- what was the role of Lieutenant-Colonel Pesic, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see the following page in Serbian. Blagoje Pesic was a staff member. And, as far as I know, from those meetings, he followed these logistical issues that had to do with the reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see the or any report that he prepared in respect to the reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any one report. He drafted those reports for the staff, and it was the staff that analysed all the activities of the reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let us look at P1055.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the last document General Lukic was referring to Mr. Pesic and Mr. Stojanovic visiting the reserve police squads, and that was at the meeting on the 17th of February. This is a document dated the 16th of February, the day before, and it's a report on the visit of the meeting with the reserve police commander. If we look at the end, just -- let's go to the end quickly. We see that it is indicated that the report was made by Captain Blagoje Pesic. Not signed, but you see his name there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And now I'd like us to go to page 3 of the document in e-court, both in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You just told us that Captain Pesic followed the logistical issues involved with the reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think it's the third paragraph on your page. You see it describes the meetings, and he says: "The meetings were held by Major-General Momcilo Stojanovic, deputy minister of the public security department, it is -- and a member of the minister's staff, and Captain Blagoje Pesic, officer in charge of organisation and functioning of the reserve police squads" -- it should be "squads," I think; you corrected us -- "in Kosovo." The police in Kosovo, you would agree with me now, Mr. Djordjevic, were responsible for the organisation and functioning of the reserve police squads? Not just the logistics?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the umpteenth time I have to respond to this question. Here is a report where Captain Pesic, with General Stojanovic, who held all those meetings, so here is the report that they are drafting. In this report, there's not a single case where a crime was committed by an RPO member. Had there been a single crime, they would have put it there, and the appropriate measures would have been taken against the perpetrator. So I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not yet talking about crimes. I'm just showing you this document - which you say is created by Major-General Stojanovic and Captain Pesic - showing you what they -- how they are designating Captain Pesic a member of the MUP staff in Kosovo. And I'm suggesting to you -- asking you that having seen this, do you not agree that the police in Kosovo were responsible for the organisation and functioning of the reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the role the police here is that it was preparing the reserve police squads for the defence against the terrorists. And in this sense, the police was duty-bound to equip them with appropriate weapons and communications equipment, to train them, and to organise their defence, to set it up, the trenches, or whatever was necessary for them to defend themselves. And to my mind, that was the role of the police. Those were not organisational units of the MUP, in which case you would have the MUP say to a squad from one village, You should go to another village and perform a task there. The task of those police personnel was to train those people, to enable them to defend themselves against the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't agree with what you see here in the document, that Captain Pesic was the officer in charge of organisation and functioning of reserve police stations? You don't agree with what they have written here?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree that he was responsible for the logistics aspect, to make sure that those police squads are able to respond to any terrorist acts. But Blagoje Pesic could not take members of the reserve police squad from one area and transfer them to another area to use them as he saw fit. Their existence was related only to their village or even part of their village, and their task was simply to defend themselves against the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let us look at page 5 in the B/C/S. Page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you informed -- this is a chart with a breakdown of the weaponry involved in this programme. Were you aware that, by then, some 64.000 weapons had been distributed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time when this report was drafted, I was in Belgrade. These are the obligations of the staff, and this is what the staff is working on with its members. I never received this report the way I see it here, or indeed in any other form or shape. So as regards these issues, I was not really informed about it. I didn't know that Momcilo Stojanovic was going down there to hold these meetings together with Blagoje Pesic and what the agenda was. Those were not issues within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You did not know. That is your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's get back to P85. If we could look at the third page in English, and I think it's the last page in B/C/S. Sorry, I think it's the penultimate page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At this meeting, which I think you said when you were first asked about it -- well, we saw it earlier, it involved all the leading members of the MUP of Serbia discussing the plans, the forthcoming plans. You see here one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine bullet points from top -- from the bottom in English, and I think it's the same in B/C/S. The Minister Stojiljkovic in your presence saying: "Approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary." We have also heard from SUP chief Cvetic that the incorporation of volunteers into the police force was illegal. What did the minister mean when he told all of you leading police officers that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant. Here we can see what he said, and he said approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when we assess this to be necessary. This is what he said. And it's his order, or his vision of things in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doesn't sound like not only an illegal order, but a very, very dangerous order to implement. Does it sound that way to you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister is in charge of the use of the police reserve force. The reserve force of the police could not be engaged or used without an appropriate decision by the minister. On the eve of the war, when Serbia was under tremendous pressure, this is what he said, and this is what is recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does it sound to you, as expressed, as minuted here, to be an order to do something which is illegal and also dangerous?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not illegal to use, to engage the reserve force. The engagement of the reserve force is not illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it illegal to engage volunteers into the reserve force? Let's not play games, this is what the minister is saying: "Approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary." Wasn't that illegal?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke about this in very restrictive terms, so at the time when war was imminent. He did not allow the engagement or the use of volunteers as volunteers. This is what it says here. He allowed it only in exceptional circumstances that, acting with care, those people who may want to fight or to be engaged, involved in this, could do so through the reserve police force. As soon as those persons are admitted to the reserve police force, they are no longer in the status of volunteers, but they become regular police or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- reserve police force, and they are entitled to everything that the reserve police force has, all the rights. So the volunteers were not engaged. They could be engaged in exceptional circumstances, based on this order of his, and be admitted as members of the reserve police force and then be engaged. And this is not illegal as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't it people who volunteered and wanted to fight, as you put it, these volunteers, weren't there procedures in place for them to be engaged by the VJ, by the army, but police work was something entirely different, and incorporating volunteers was illegal?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police has the right to use its reserve force. There are thousands of members of the reserve police force. Now, how the police are going to use an individual, how to register him, admit him as a member of the reserve force, it's a different issue. The police did not admit volunteers and use them as volunteers as part of some units of that sort, and they were not engaged in any other kind of work. So first those persons became members of the reserve force, and then they were sent to execute their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, I think, that you issued a follow-up order to the conclusions at this meeting. Do you recall that? That you sent an order which --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were shown that as well. Let's look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the order you were shown, 18th of February, 1999, your dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to page -- to item 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is your order based on the minister's instructions about volunteers. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order to the secretariats, but this order differs from the order that was presented that way at the minister’s. So the secretariats are ordered to step up their operative work and to take other measures in order to check and register and control the volunteer and paramilitary units and their members. The essence of controlling all these categories lies in the fact that those units would go to the territory of Kosovo in an uncontrolled manner, and there they would loot and commit other crimes. In the previous period, we have seen isolated dispatches where orders were issued prohibiting the entry of such units to Kosovo, and this order goes along the same lines. The purpose is to prevent them from entering Kosovo where they would commit crimes. So this is what this order is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you go back to the front page, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- is based on the minister's decisions as to how you should treat these paramilitaries and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that this dispatch followed partly from the orders issued at the meeting, but also from the obligations that we had as part of the general preparations for the defence of the country. So the air-strikes and war were imminent, and this dispatch, in fact, contains the orders to the secretariats to prepare for war. One of the items is the one that we've just discussed, item 7, which deals with the issue of volunteer and paramilitary units, but the essence, what this is all about, is to exert control over them and to prevent them from going to Kosovo where they would commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want you to note, Mr. Djordjevic, that this is dispatch number 312 of the 18th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P702.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Probably it's a little difficult to read. This is a dispatch of the minister of the 24th of March, 1999, the eve of the -- of the NATO intervention and also the eve of when most of the crimes charged in this indictment, in the indictment here, were committed. If you read the first paragraph, and you will see that it's sent to almost all the important police in the country. This is, all senior police in the country. He says that it is necessary to intensify the enforcement of measures that were ordered as per our dispatch number 312 of the 18th of February, 1999, he is referencing to the dispatch you sent which he calls "our dispatch." You see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see item 5? It's probably difficult to read. Item 5, I think, is on the second page of your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it could be brought up into better focus, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that's legible. The minister instructs an intensification of your order, which he calls "our order," you shall register all volunteer and paramilitary units and their members and keep them under control in case you might need to engage them.
