Come now, Mr. Djordjevic, yourself and the minister were acting and planning in contemplation of using volunteers and paramilitary units as soon as the NATO intervention began; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. In the dispatch, in my dispatch, it says clearly that they should be registered and controlled. But the objective was not to engage them, to use them. Here in this dispatch it says "for their possible engagement." It is a dispatch that is sent directly from the minister. Now, why this was ordered, I don't know. But what I do know is that not a single volunteer or paramilitary unit on the order of the minister as it is described here did not go to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to this topic, you seem very, very familiar with what was going on there in Kosovo. And, you know, so many other topics that I've asked you about, you know nothing about Kosovo. Mr. Djordjevic, this order says "... in case you might need to engage them." And he is sending this order to the leadership of the police. Weren't you then aware of a plan to use volunteers and paramilitaries after the NATO intervention began?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no plan and no one volunteer unit was deployed or used in the area of Kosovo and Metohija as is said here. That is, not one volunteer or paramilitary unit was used down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you must have been receiving reports and being involved in the management of the police and their activities down there for you to say that with such conviction.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that has nothing to do with it. I wasn't involved in any plans regarding the plans of the police for Kosovo and Metohija, nor did I issue any instructions to use any police unit that was deployed to Kosovo and Metohija. I never issued instructions to either a commander or the Chief of Staff or the chief of the SUP, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, well, let me show you some other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at P889.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the 16th of February again. We can probably refer to that period as a planning phase. And this is a VJ order. And please, sir, if you could note the number -- reference number to the top left-hand corner, it's in handwriting, 455. The 455 series, and this is number 1. And it is an order for the destruction or the breaking apart of forces, that is, STS forces in Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo. Let's look at -- firstly, you see -- I think we have to go to another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 4 in the English, and we have to try to work together to find the appropriate page in B/C/S. Item 2. Page 3 in B/C/S. Yes, I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It refers to: "In coordinated action of the forces of MUP of the Republic of Serbia, block, break-up, and destroy STS in the general sector of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo. At the same time, secure the state border with the republic of Albania and Macedonia, prevent the infiltration of the STS by closing off the axes leading from the Republic of Albania and the Republic of Macedonia, and secure military facilities, communications, and control of territory." You see, two paragraphs down, I don't want to have to read all of it. It says: "Later on, secure the passability of the major roads and full control of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Engage armed non-Siptars to secure military facilities and communications and to defend places with non-Siptar populations." You see here, Mr. Djordjevic, the plan for the operations involve the use of the armed Serbs in Kosovo. Does this remind you of what the circumstances or what the operations were at the time? Or may I withdraw that question and put it this way: Does this remind you that the operations in Kosovo involved the use of armed ethnic Serbs supporting the MUP and the VJ in these operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we can read here. But these documents, which I've now seen for the first time, have nothing to do with me. I haven't partaken in the drafting of this document, nor do I know who drafted it and under whose instructions. I suppose that they had orders from their command. But the way it stands here, I have nothing whatsoever to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I show you another one. And this one is in reference to the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at P1393.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The combat report to the 3rd Army by Major-General Lazarevic, the commander of the Pristina Corps, 25th of April, 1999. If you look at page 2 of the English and stay on page 1 in Serbian, in item 2.1, the first paragraph of that page in English, and it's item 2.1. You can see that: "Operations of combing the terrain and breaking up the STS continue in line with the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." And it goes on to describe what is happening further. The system, the structure, involving the Joint Command responsible for the -- for coordinating the activities of the VJ and the MUP in these operations, remained in place during the war when these -- the crimes we are concerned about were committed. Does this, Mr. Djordjevic, remind you of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Stamp read a sentence from this document and then gives his conclusions that have nothing to with the document. Please, take a look at this question. He started by quoting the first sentence and then what followed was a digression and some conclusions of his, and all that has nothing to do with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you rephrase your question, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document says, Mr. Djordjevic, that the operations shall continue in line with a decision of the Joint Command. Does this not remind you that during operations in Kosovo in 1999 when the crimes we are concerned about -- concerned with here were committed, the Joint Command was still in existence?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, several months before this combat report, which was drafted in late April, so several months earlier, I had nothing whatsoever to do with the activities down there or with the plans or combat reports. How it came and that somebody used this term "Joint Command" and why they did so, I cannot know. Maybe they meant "joint action," and perhaps this term was coined in a haphazard fashion and then used subsequently. But I'm in no way familiar with the existence of such a command down there or what they're doing -- what they were doing. At that point in time, my tasks were altogether different. Who wrote that and why is for that person to answer. And I cannot provide and explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P969.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Joint Command order of the 15th of April, 1999. And take note the number, 455-151. And if you could go down to item 2, "Tasks of the Pristina Corps": "With reinforcements and the armed non-Siptar population in Kosovo and Metohija, the Pristina Corps shall support MUP forces in breaking up and destroying STS in its zone of responsibility." You, General Djordjevic, you don't know about this is your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In preparing for this case, you must have seen dozens of orders from the Joint Command in 1999. Do you recall seeing them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw several orders of this kind with such a letterhead and what was done within the Pristina Corps, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we may move on. You testified about being in Pristina on the 18th of April, 1999, or thereabouts, and General Pavkovic showed you a document relating to the resubordination of the MUP to the VJ. You said you didn't know anything about it and that was something for the minister. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, please, I said and -- what I said is recorded in the transcript. So at the moment when Pavkovic called General Lukic to come and see him, I went there and he showed me that paper. At the moment when he showed it to me, I read it. It was one sentence, and I said that we had no idea about that, that I had come from Belgrade that day. And I know about the documents and all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me that this has become the practice on the part of Mr. Stamp to interpret -- to interpret things very freely and falsely. So whenever he quotes, I would ask him to quote accurately. He falsely quoted Mr. Djordjevic to have said that he knows nothing about resubordination. And you all heard what the accused said. So when my learned friend quotes, I do ask him to quote accurately rather than retell it in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, firstly, I wasn't quoting, I was summarising. And secondly, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection is that you do not summarise accurately, worse than that, at times you summarise misleadingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And looking at the record of what I summarised, I would submit that I summarised accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Attention is particularly drawn to the sentence that he said he had -- "we have no knowledge -- I beg your pardon. You said you did not know anything about it, that being resubordination, and that was something for the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I said to him General Pavkovic showed you a document relating to resubordination of the VJ and the MUP. And you said you didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I said General Djordjevic [sic] showed you a document relating to the resubordination of the MUP and the VJ, and you said you didn't know anything about it, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue is, is that a fair summary of the particular passage of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I submit it is. He said he did not know anything about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say "it" meant the document, not resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you can see here that there may be some ambiguity in what was said by Mr. Stamp. What he puts is, I think, an accurate section of the evidence that Mr. Djordjevic said he knew nothing about the document that dealt with resubordination. Now, in the particular way the sentence is expressed, I can see that it could be understood the way you understood it, that is, that he knew nothing about resubordination. Mr. Stamp says he intended it to mean that he knew nothing about the document that was shown to him. I think, in those circumstances, it is not the case that Mr. Stamp is in any way seeking to mislead the witness. But you will realise, of course, Mr. Stamp, that in some of these matters which are quite material, there does need to be care by you so that you are quoting accurately or fairly, not necessarily precisely the words, but if you are summarising, that you are doing so fairly. And there have been times when you have been very loose in your reference back. It's of concern to the Defence. If you could pay attention to that in future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. If I may say something more, the accused answered to that question, and he himself said that it was wrong. Namely with regard to the phrasing of the question. And that's why I would ask for quotations to be accurate rather than to be put in such a way as to be ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, when you returned to Belgrade, inquire as to what were the reasons for the VJ to be pressing this issue of resubordination?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch of General Ojdanic which I saw at General Pavkovic's office, was something that I informed the minister. And he said that he would take care of it, probably with Mr. Ojdanic. And after my -- after this information I gave to the minister, based on what I saw later, there was never an act from the Chief of Staff sent to the minister containing a request for units or organs of the intern of the MUP to be resubordinated. That's all I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I was asking whether or not you asked about or discovered the reasons why the VJ wanted resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P888. If we could just go to the end to see that it is signed, or I could just tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is an order, or this is a report by commander of the 3rd Army, Pavkovic, which he sent to the Supreme Command of the 25th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the first page in English and look at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll just read it: He says. "The security regime in the territory has not taken root in the spirit of the law and on the basis of the proclaimed state of war. The best example is the operation of joint check-points manned by MUP and the military police units where there are frequent altercations because MUP members condone or openly permit evident criminal activities and plunder committed by their fellow MUP members, as well as civilians, resulting in the misappropriation of a vast number of motor vehicles, technical goods, and other resources from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." Look at paragraph 4 on the next page: "It has been established beyond doubt, and we have already reported on it in regular combat and other reports, that due to the non-compliance with the resubordination orders, some MUP members and to a considerable extent entire smaller units which operate independently on the ground, are committing serious crimes against the Siptar civilian population in settlements or refugee shelters - murder, rape, plunder, robbery, aggravated theft, et cetera, and they then purposely attribute or plan to attribute these crimes to units and individuals of the VJ." Now, were you aware of these complaints being made by the leadership of the VJ about the conduct of the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such information has ever reached me. And I would say that on the 4th of May, we attended a meeting with the president of the SRJ, that is, a considerable time after the resubordination order and a month and 40 days after the start of the war, and General Pavkovic had a briefing, and General Lukic too, and the result of that meeting was a document about good work and good results and no problem existing between the police and the military was mentioned. On the 10th of July when the minister organised a visit of the Chief of General Staff, Mr. Ojdanic, the units of -- we heard that the units of the police and the military, under very difficult conditions, operated jointly to general satisfaction. So we have the opinion of the Chief of General Staff and the minister that the relations were all right and without any problems, but opposed to that there is this letter by General Pavkovic from roughly the same time who is generally pointing out some things and blaming somebody else for every one of these things. There has never been any written document from the VJ that arrived at the ministry, certainly it never reached me, but I'm sure that it never reached the minister either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to the meeting of the 9th of July later on. You see the last thing that General Pavkovic recommended in this letter?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal of measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. "In light of the above said and particularly the consequences already in evidence which could, however, become much more important, the Supreme Command should take urgent measures, falling within its jurisdiction, to resubordinate the units and organs of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in the spirit of the constitution and existing laws and in accordance with the proclaimed state of war, or annul the order on the resubordination and leave the command and commanding of the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo through the Joint Command as has so far been the case." Again, General Pavkovic it referring to the existence of the Joint Command as far forward as the 25th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the -- what is contained in the proposal of measures and what he recommends to the Supreme Command by way of some urgent measures, I don't know that as of the time when this letter was purportedly sent on the 25th of May until the end of the war, the Supreme Command never talked to the minister to highlight those problems that General Pavkovic is writing about here. So the issue of reattachment or lack thereof or any other allegations in this letter was never raised. Now, as to when and why this letter was written, well, also this, what it says, the MUP staff "through the Joint Command," what the author wanted to say is really unclear to me. He should have expressed himself more clearly, what he meant when he said the Joint Command. Now, if I were to try and get into his mind and to interpret what he wanted to say, I'm really not in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember where you were on the 1st of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll is it -- we'll get to that shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, if you are moving on. We'll break now and resume at 6.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was -- sorry, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was Mr. Stojiljkovic removed from office by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think sometime around the 10th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you remained in your position until 2001?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you must note that on the 5th of October, 2000, the democratic changes occurred and then the government in Serbia was re-organised until the new cabinet was appointed. There were three co-minsters, and I was the chief of the public security department. When the new cabinet was established, I was appointed one of the advisors to the minister; Sreten Lukic was appointed the chief of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: None of that but for the yes I asked you about. Please focus on my questions and answer them directly. I say this because of the time. Incidentally, you told us that you sent a letter to clarify your position to a news outlet. Can you remember the date when you sent that letter, the month or the year?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall. I can't remember this time. But I think that you can see from your documents when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I tell you that it was in May 2004, would you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would disagree or can you --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you gave somebody the letter to post for you. Did you write on the envelope on the letter your --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you asked the person to post it from Moscow?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I addressed a letter, I put it in a larger envelope that did not have any markings on it, he took it, and then he posted it from Moscow to the address.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P -- sorry, document 05223. And that is P1472.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this what you wrote on the envelope?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that the front of the envelope, the addressee, the editor of the magazine that you sent it to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look at the back.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the return address that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said at that time you were living in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you using your own name where you lived? That is, did you go by the name Vlastimir Djordjevic at the place in Montenegro where you lived?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was it in Montenegro? What was the address in Montenegro that you lived at?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived in several addresses. I don't know -- well, I lived in several addresses. It was not just one place of residence. I moved from one to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at 05225. And that is 1474.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have already identified this document as your letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at page 8 of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think maybe for your purposes you want to start with the paragraph -- with the last paragraph of page 7, just read that. And when you are ready, you could move to page 8.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to read? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last paragraph of page 7.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister ordered me it to issue an order to prevent -- yes, he did issue those two orders that envisaged the use of fire-arms to prevent the arrival of citizens to the protest rally. And later on when several hundred thousand demonstrators gathered there, he issued an order to me to order the liquidation of a bulldozer driver who was breaking through the police cordons. He issued this order to me, and I, of course, refused to obey. And then after the demonstrations --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So these are two orders that you refused to obey? If you look at page 8 now, the top of page 8 of this document. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we are on this document, maybe I should ask one or two things about it. If you look at page 7 in English and 6 in B/C/S, near to the top of page 7 and just about the middle in B/C/S, you wrote: "I did not know anything about civilian casualties in Kosovo and Metohija at the time of the bombing, whether there were any and at which locations. Nobody informed me about that, nor was it their duty to inform me." I think you admitted here in the course of your testimony that at least you knew about the victims in Podujevo, so this statement that you knew nothing about civilian casualties, which you included in your letter to the Serbian people, is not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was written several years after I had left. And in the meantime, there were lots of various reports in various newspapers. At that time, I wrote this fully aware of the fact that there were some defects here or some elements that were based on my feeling, I may have exaggerated my role here or there, but there are some inaccuracies. For instance, at page 3, now that I have had a closer look at it, I see that I said that the anti-terrorist activities started on the 1st of July, whereas they actually started one month later. So I really, here, am --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm asking you about what you said, that you did not know anything about any casualties. That was a deliberate misrepresentation, was it not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, sir, I wrote this replying to articles in the newspapers there. Here, I'm giving evidence to this Trial Chamber. And what I am saying here is something that's very clear. Basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what you said there -- what you said there -- and I just want you to focus on that statement. What you said there is not true, and you deliberately misrepresented that, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention that event for -- I don't know for which reason. It isn't like I did something and -- but simply I didn't show it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's important what's said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask that question again. I have to move on. But you haven't answered it. There's another thing I noticed in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me look at page 10 in English. Sorry, page 11 in English. And that is also the last part in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you retired on the 3rd of May. And I think you are telling us here that you were dismissed. Is that your evidence here, that you were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I retired. I wasn't replaced or dismissed. I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember telling this Court on two occasions, the first day you testified, that you were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never stated that to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard another statement by Mr. Stamp, and I repeat my request to him, that when he does so, he should correctly quote what he is quoting and state what he is quoting. He may have misunderstood some things, but this clearly says "I retired." And in the direct examination, he never said that he was dismissed. He was saying about his retirement, that he retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At 9398.6 of his testimony on the 1st of December, line 6, he said, in answer to Mr. Djurdjic: "Yes, this is a definite decision for me. It was passed by the minister of interior, and it says that I was dismissed altogether on the 3rd of May 2001." Later on, in response to another question from Mr. Djurdjic at line 14: "At the moment when I was dismissed from the position of the -- of assistant minister and when I was appointed counsellor to the minister, the minister decided that I should be a member of the coordinating body for south of Serbia." This is a different dismissal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think there are other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what I think, since this objection is raised, I should put on the record that you were telling this Court on that day that you were never aware that your dismissal was being contemplated until the 3rd. The Prosecution had put on its exhibit list to question you, your letter requesting dismissal. And Mr. Djurdjic, at 9764, in light of that history, asked you this question just before the end of your examination-in-chief: "Thank you. Under Article 41 of the ministry of -- or rather, of the Law of Internal Affairs, you went into early retirement. Did you; and, if so, when did you sign the request to retire?" Up until Mr. Djurdjic put those words in your mouth, most probably having seen the Prosecution's list, you did not say that you made a request to retire. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there must be a hundred questions here. The first question is my dismissal from the position of assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, the question is this: You have already told us, Mr. Djordjevic, that you never said so. So the question now is this: Do you recall that you first referred to sending a letter requesting retirement after Mr. Djurdjic told you that in the question that he asked you? Do you remember that? You remember, the answer is yes; if you do not remember, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, sir. This isn't just about yes or no. I want to repeat: I worked on the 3rd of October, and I was 350 kilometres away from Belgrade. On that day, the decision about my retirement was passed. On that evening, Sreten Lukic called me to come because I was a pensioner then. I come on the 4th, he gives me an application for early retirement, and then I signed both the application and the decision about my retirement. That's the only truth. Nothing else. So I did not, on the 30th or whichever date is mentioned in the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date, I didn't sign an application for early retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, you refuse to answer the question I put to you.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not refusing anything. Come on. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Djurdjic, this is a matter you deal with in re-examination if that is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. But it's recorded wrongly in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, clearly there are minds torn about this issue. We do not want to hear your account of the facts, we want to hear the witness's at this point. You will have full opportunity to deal with it with the witness in re-examination. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the letter to Mr. -- to the newspaper, if I can find it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 1474. Page 7 in English, page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is on perhaps what some people would call the most important issue you could cover in this letter. It's the penultimate paragraph in the B/C/S and the third paragraph in the English: "I first found out about the refrigerator truck with bodies in the Danube after being informed by the chief minister" -- sorry, excuse me -- "by the chief of Bor, SUP, Caslav Golubovic. He informed me that there were several scores of bodies in refrigerator truck, and I immediately proposed that the complete criminal process be conducted there." To which you reply that there were no conditions to do so there. "Immediately after that conversation, I informed the minister about everything. And half an hour later, he issued an order for me -- order to me for the bodies to be transported to Belgrade for autopsy and further criminal processing." I repeat, in this letter you said: "In respect to these corpses, the minister issued an order to me for the bodies to be transported to Belgrade for autopsy and for further criminal processing." I already read to you what you said when you opened in January of this year at transcript 240, page 240, and also what you said to us at transcript 9721, a third version where you said that the order of the minister was that after routine procedures the bodies should be buried in the vicinity where found. Three accounts. But let's focus on this one that you sent to the people in Serbia. That, again, was a misrepresentation of what you did after you discovered or you were told about the truck with the bodies, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these things should be held apart. What was written for the newspapers and another thing are the details about which I'm speaking here. So then, when I was called up by the head of the SUP, Golubovic, he told me that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please stop there. I do not wish and I do not ask that you go to explain the history. I have read to you three different accounts. I want to know -- the question is: Is the account that I just read, that you wrote to the newspapers, a deliberate misrepresentation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote for the papers is presented basically the way it was. There are some details, which I didn't mention then, but I'm giving evidence now about all these facts. I don't think that the most important thing is what is said here, and what I wrote for the papers. I haven't left out anything here. When I give an account of my actions, that followed this first information. But this is an opportunity here to discuss all that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. If we could return to your defiance of orders that you received from the minister which you didn't agree with. You recall that you testified in a trial in Serbia, testified via videolink on the 20 -- on a date in July this year? 26th of June. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think this is Exhibit 6010. Sorry, 65 ter number 601.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have it here. This is a transcript of your testimony on that day, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move to page 10. I think that is page 12 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you say again here that you were given the order on the 5th of October to shoot, or rather, to issue the order to kill the excavator operator who was driving, and then: "I entered into a fierce conflict with him and refused to obey that order in the presence of General Zekovic. Therefore, he could issue all kinds of orders, whichever he wanted, and the problem was whether these tasks could be carried out or not. I found that the task I was given was completely in accordance with the regulations that members of the service were entitled to do, and I issued the order for this task." I believe, here, what you want to say is that -- or what you are saying is that you refused -- you refused to obey this order to shoot the excavator operator because it was not in accordance with the regulations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Since we are on this document, before I close it, I'll probably come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at page 15. Another thing I noticed. And page 15 in English is page 18 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this -- in that case, Mr. Djordjevic, you were aware of your obligation to tell the Court the truth, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was an investigation or a trial of persons who were tried for the murder of three American citizens of Kosovo Albanian descent?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are asked by the Deputy Prosecutor, and it's at page 15, whether you ever met Popovic, who was one of the accused, in Kosovo or elsewhere. And in your answer you say: "He may have seen me, but I don't know if I saw him. I cannot be sure. But I was down there in 1998, so it was possible for him to see me and to meet me. In 1999 I was there only once with the minister." Well, we know from your evidence here that in 1999 you were down a few more times than once. And I suggest to you that when you testified in June, you say -- you must have known that. Didn't you deliberately misrepresent the amount of times you were in Kosovo in 1999 to the war crimes court of Belgrade when you testified in June this year?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no reason to misrepresent that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about any explanations. I will get to that later. The record here says that you told them that you were there only once and this was material to the issues in the trial. And I asked you if that was a deliberate misrepresentation to the Belgrade court.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that, I probably made a mistake. I have no reason to -- not to tell that court that I was there two or three times, as many times as I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a little bit after the time, Your Honours, I was wondering if it's convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we must draw to a close today, Mr. Stamp. I know it's at the end of a day that has been tiring for both yourself and the witness. Can I ask how you see your timing?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I should be finished sometime in the course of Monday. I say this -- and I do not want to get into any issues with the witness, but I -- it depends on whether or not I can control the response to the question. I do have a lot of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we can I assist you. We've made arrangements this afternoon to assist you by arranging to sit tomorrow from 10.00 until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That there will be a break of an hour for lunch between 1.30 and 2.30. That will give you a longer time, but it will give both you and the witness a more manageable day. Now, with that having been done, the Chamber expects that you will be able to finish by the end of the first session on Monday, so as to enable re-examination to be dealt with. If you can keep that in mind as you plan tomorrow and plan over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the Court I rises, I'm sorry, I think I left a little bit of housekeeping undone. 06010, identified by the witness, to be the transcript. Could that be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript of the evidence given, was it in June or July of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In June. 26th of June, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I'm unclear at this moment. We have the envelope in which a letter was sent to a magazine from Moscow. Do we have the letter as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What exhibit number is the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's P1474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, tomorrow, to accommodate that different sitting time, we've got to move courts, and we will be in Courtroom II tomorrow, and we commence at 10.00. We will adjourn now until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of December, 2009, at 10.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
